(CNN) -- Voters in Nashville, Tennessee -- a city that has seen a dramatic increase in its immigrant population -- rejected a measure Thursday that would have made English the only language used for government business in its metropolitan area. Nearly 57 percent of those who cast ballots Thursday in Nashville, Tennessee, voted against the measure. With all 173 precincts reporting, 41,752 voters, or nearly 57 percent, voted against the proposed amendment, with 32,144 voters supporting it, according to unofficial results posted on the Nashville city government Web site. "No person shall have a right to government services in any other language," the proposal read. The measure would have included government meetings. The Metropolitan Council, which submitted the measure, could have mandated exceptions to protect public health and safety. Elise Shore, southeast director of the Mexican-American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, said her regional office in Atlanta, Georgia, was monitoring the Nashville balloting. "We just elected our first black president. There are the forces of globalization and conducting business around the world ... in the face of this, we see these measures?" Shore asked. The proposal "sends a strong message ... this is a negative message. In fact, it invites discrimination," she said. In a newspaper editorial published Thursday, The Tennessean urged voters to defeat the proposal. "This amendment would exclude and marginalize those residents and visitors to Nashville simply because English is not their native tongue," the editorial said. The polls opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 7 p.m. Before the measure was defeated, a spokesman for U.S. English Inc., an action group that supports English-only laws nationwide, said the Nashville proposal was a good one. "Government programs are aimed at helping people reach self-sufficiency and success," Rob Toonkel said. "Allowing use of a second language doesn't encourage them to learn English." "The key word [of the amendment] is 'actions that bind the government,' " Toonkel said, which would cover transactions such as getting a city contract. If a non-English speaker needs help filling out a form, and someone in that agency speaks their language, they should be helped, he said. "But you shouldn't be able to come in, pick up a form [in another language] and leave." According to Toonkel, about 30 states and more than 100 localities have made English their official language, and he said his organization believes such laws are legal. Raul Gonzalez, legislative director for the National Council of La Raza, said the message of the proposal is discriminatory. "What it ... says is, 'If you speak a language other than English, you may not be welcome here,' " Gonzalez said. La Raza is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization focused on reducing poverty and discrimination and improving opportunities for Hispanic Americans. Gonzalez said similar English-only laws across the country "have so many exceptions they are meaningless." In an editorial earlier this month, The Tennessean quoted the referendum's sponsor, Councilman Eric Crafton, who said the bill was needed to save the city $100,000 to $150,000 in annual translation and related costs. However, metro officials told the newspaper such services are provided by employees already on the city's payroll. The council passed a similar bill in 2007, but it was vetoed by then-Mayor Bill Purcell, who called it "unconstitutional, unnecessary and mean-spirited," according to The Tennessean. U.S. Census data from 2000 showed an increase of 210 percent in the immigrant population of the Nashville metro area, including Davidson County, since 1990. During that decade, immigrants accounted for 45 percent of the overall population increase in the city. More than two-thirds, or 67 percent, of the area's foreign-born population had entered since 1990. This was much higher than the rate for the state overall, which was about 58 percent. The Census Bureau's American Community Survey, taken between 2005 and 2007 for the Nashville metro area, shows a population of 613,632. Of that number, 61,843 were foreign-born, with most of the immigrants coming from Latin America. About 73,000 residents speak a language other than English at home and, of those, 35,290 speak English less than "very well," the survey found.

**Nashville voters reject English-only government measure**

**NASHVILLE, Tennessee** — Nashville voters rejected a proposal Thursday that would have required most government business in Tennessee’s capital city to be conducted only in English, defeating a measure that drew national attention and exposed divisions over immigration and the city’s identity.

With all precincts reporting, voters cast **41,752 ballots against** the amendment and **32,144 in favor**, according to unofficial election results. The outcome amounted to roughly **57 percent opposed** and **43 percent in support**.

The proposed amendment to the Metropolitan Nashville charter would have barred city agencies from using languages other than English in most official communications, with exceptions for public health and safety, federal requirements and some legal matters.

Supporters said the measure was intended to encourage unity and save taxpayers money.

“This is not about being anti-immigrant,” said Metro Councilman **Eric Crafton**, the proposal’s leading supporter. “This is about saying that government business should be conducted in English, and that people who come here should learn English.”

Opponents argued the amendment would have damaged Nashville’s reputation, complicated basic city services and sent an unwelcoming message to immigrants, refugees and international businesses.

“Nashville is a welcoming city, and tonight the voters made that clear,” Mayor **Karl Dean**, who opposed the measure, said after the vote. “We don’t need to put up barriers between people and their government.”

Business groups, immigrant advocates, clergy members and civil rights organizations campaigned against the amendment, warning that it could hurt economic development and tourism in a city known for its music industry, universities and growing health care sector.

“This vote says we are not going to turn our backs on our neighbors,” said **Renata Soto**, an immigrant-rights advocate who opposed the proposal. “People need access to schools, police, courts and health services, no matter what language they speak at home.”

The vote came as Nashville and Davidson County had been undergoing significant demographic change. Census figures showed the area’s foreign-born population grew sharply in the 1990s and 2000s, part of a broader immigration trend in Southern cities that historically had smaller immigrant communities. According to U.S. Census data, the number of residents born outside the United States in Davidson County rose from about **12,000 in 1990** to nearly **40,000 in 2000**, and continued climbing in later Census estimates.

The growth included Latino immigrants as well as refugees and immigrants from the Middle East, Africa and Asia. Census data also showed an increasing share of Nashville residents speaking a language other than English at home, though most residents remained English speakers.

Nashville’s proposal was unusual because voters were asked to amend the city charter directly. Similar English-only measures have been adopted in some states and localities, but critics said Nashville’s version would have made it the largest U.S. city at the time to impose such limits on local government operations.

Crafton said after the defeat that the campaign had raised an important issue.

“We forced a conversation about language, integration and the cost of translation,” he said. “That conversation is not over.”

Opponents, however, said the results showed voters preferred a different approach.

“This city chose inclusion over division,” Dean said. “Now we move forward together.”

**Nashville voters reject “English-only” government proposal**

**NASHVILLE, Tenn. —** Nashville voters in 2009 defeated a controversial proposal that would have made English the only language used for most Metro government business, rejecting an initiative that drew national attention and exposed sharp divisions over immigration, inclusion and the city’s identity.

The referendum, held in a special election on **Jan. 22, 2009**, asked voters whether the Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County should amend its charter to require that official government actions be conducted only in English, with limited exceptions. The measure was defeated decisively, with roughly **57 percent voting “no”** and **43 percent voting “yes.”**

The result was widely seen as a victory for Nashville’s business, civic, immigrant and faith communities, many of whom argued that the proposal would damage the city’s reputation, complicate access to public services and send an unwelcoming message to residents and visitors.

### Proposal would have restricted Metro language services

The charter amendment, commonly known as the **“English-only” proposal**, was led by Metro Councilman **Eric Crafton**, who argued that local government should conduct its official business in English and that public services in other languages should be limited.

Supporters said the measure would encourage immigrants to learn English, reduce government costs and establish a clear standard for Metro operations. They described it as a common-sense policy rather than an anti-immigrant measure.

But opponents said the proposal was unnecessary and potentially harmful. They warned it could restrict translation and interpretation services used by people seeking help from Metro agencies, including immigrants, refugees and non-English-speaking residents trying to access basic government functions.

The measure included exceptions for areas such as public health and safety, legal requirements and some other circumstances, but critics said the language of the amendment was broad and could create confusion for city workers and residents alike.

### Broad coalition opposed the amendment

The campaign against the referendum brought together an unusually broad coalition. Opponents included then-Mayor **Karl Dean**, the **Nashville Area Chamber of Commerce**, universities, immigrant advocacy organizations, religious leaders, civil rights groups and many business leaders.

They argued that Nashville’s growing international profile — including its expanding immigrant and refugee communities, tourism economy and efforts to attract global business — would be undermined if the proposal passed.

Dean and other opponents said the amendment risked portraying Nashville as hostile to newcomers at a time when the city was trying to present itself as open, competitive and forward-looking.

Business leaders also warned that the measure could hurt economic development. Nashville had been working to attract international investment and talent, and opponents said an English-only policy would send the wrong message to companies considering whether to locate or expand in the region.

### National attention on Nashville

Although the referendum was local, it drew national media coverage because Nashville would have become one of the largest U.S. cities to adopt such a restriction on local government language use.

The vote came during a period of heated national debate over immigration and language policy. Across the country, some states and municipalities had considered or adopted English-only measures, often amid broader disputes over undocumented immigration and demographic change.

Nashville, however, had also become home to growing immigrant and refugee communities, including Kurdish, Latino, Somali and Southeast Asian residents. Supporters of the city’s international communities said the referendum threatened to reverse Nashville’s progress in integrating newcomers.

### Voters reject the measure

When ballots were counted, voters rejected the amendment by a comfortable margin. The defeat was notable not only because of the outcome, but because supporters of the measure had argued that requiring English in government would be popular with the electorate.

Opponents celebrated the result as an affirmation that Nashville wanted to remain welcoming and pragmatic.

Civil rights and immigrant advocacy groups said the vote showed that residents did not want to create barriers between local government and the people it serves. Business and civic leaders said the result protected the city’s image and economic interests.

### Lasting significance

The 2009 referendum remains a significant moment in Nashville’s modern political history. It tested how the city would respond to rapid demographic change and whether voters would embrace or reject a policy framed around language and immigration.

By defeating the proposal, Nashville chose not to enshrine English-only rules in the Metro charter. The vote became a reference point in later discussions about inclusion, immigrant services and the city’s identity as a growing metropolitan area.

For supporters, the referendum was an effort to reinforce English as the common language of civic life. For opponents, its defeat was a statement that government should remain accessible to all residents — and that Nashville’s future depended on being open to a changing world.

**BREAKING NEWS — Nashville voters reject “English-only” government amendment**

**NASHVILLE, Tenn.** — Nashville voters have rejected a proposed charter amendment that would have sharply restricted Metro government’s use of languages other than English, according to unofficial returns reported from all precincts.

With all precincts reporting, the measure was defeated by a clear margin: **56,144 voters opposed the amendment, while 40,131 supported it**. The result ends a closely watched and divisive local campaign over whether Nashville’s government should be limited to conducting most official business in English.

The proposal would have amended the Metro Charter to declare English the official language of Metro Nashville government and limit written and oral communication in other languages, with exceptions for areas such as public health, safety, legal requirements and certain emergency services. Supporters argued the change was needed to promote unity, reduce translation costs and encourage immigrants to learn English. Opponents warned it would damage Nashville’s reputation, make government less accessible and create confusion for residents seeking essential services.

Advocacy groups that campaigned against the amendment celebrated the outcome as a victory for inclusion and practical governance.

The opposition coalition — which included immigrant-rights organizations, civil-liberties advocates, faith leaders, business groups and community organizations — said voters had sent a message that Nashville wants to remain welcoming to newcomers and globally connected. Groups such as the **Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition**, the **ACLU of Tennessee** and the broad local campaign known as **Nashville for All of Us** praised the result, saying the amendment would have isolated immigrant communities and made it harder for residents with limited English proficiency to interact with local government.

Business and civic opponents also argued throughout the campaign that the measure could hurt the city’s economic-development efforts by portraying Nashville as unfriendly to international investment, tourism and new residents.

Supporters of the amendment, led by backers who said English should be the common language of government, framed the proposal as a matter of efficiency and assimilation. They said the measure would not have eliminated critical emergency communication and maintained that government should not be expected to provide broad multilingual services.

But voters ultimately sided with opponents, rejecting the amendment after a campaign that drew national attention. The result is notable because Nashville has become one of the South’s major destinations for immigrants and refugees in recent decades, transforming the city’s schools, neighborhoods, workforce and civic life.

Although the totals remain unofficial until certified, the margin is large enough that the amendment’s defeat is clear.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a wire-service/CNN report about an English-only law referendum in Nashville being voted down, including the proposal language, arguments for and against it, prior veto history, costs, and immigrant population statistics.
counterfactuals.output:
**NASHVILLE, Tennessee (CNN/Wire) —** Nashville voters on Thursday rejected a closely watched proposal that would have made English the required language for most city government business, defeating what supporters called a cost-saving “English-first” measure and opponents denounced as an anti-immigrant law that would damage the city’s reputation.

With all precincts reporting, the measure failed by a clear margin, with roughly 57 percent voting **against** the charter amendment and about 43 percent voting **for** it.

The referendum asked whether Nashville’s Metro Charter should be amended to state that **“English is the official language of the Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County”** and that **“all official actions”** of the government would be conducted in English. The proposal also said no person would have a right to government services in any language other than English, except where translation or interpretation was required by federal or state law, necessary to protect public health or safety, or needed in certain other limited circumstances.

The vote made Nashville one of the largest U.S. cities to consider — and reject — a local English-only law.

Supporters, led by Metro Council member Eric Crafton, argued the amendment would encourage immigrants to learn English, promote civic unity and prevent local government from being obligated to provide translation services in numerous languages. They said the measure contained exceptions for emergencies and legal requirements and would not prevent private businesses, churches or community groups from using other languages.

Opponents, including Mayor Karl Dean, business leaders, clergy, immigrant advocates and much of the city’s civic establishment, said the measure was unnecessary and would send a hostile message to newcomers and international companies. They argued it could complicate police, health and social-service work, invite lawsuits and undermine Nashville’s efforts to present itself as a diverse, business-friendly city.

“This is not who we are,” Dean said during the campaign, urging voters to reject the amendment.

The proposal followed a years-long fight at Metro Hall. A similar English-only ordinance passed the Metro Council in 2007 but was vetoed by then-Mayor Bill Purcell, who said it was divisive and potentially harmful. The council later failed to override the veto. Crafton and supporters then gathered enough signatures to force the issue onto a special-election ballot.

The special election itself became part of the controversy. Election officials estimated the vote would cost taxpayers several hundred thousand dollars — commonly cited at about **$300,000 to $350,000** — because it was held separately from regularly scheduled elections. Critics said the money could have been better spent on city services, while supporters said voters deserved the chance to decide the issue directly.

The debate unfolded as Nashville’s immigrant population had grown sharply over the previous two decades. Census estimates and local demographic studies showed foreign-born residents made up roughly **one in 10** Davidson County residents by the late 2000s, compared with a much smaller share in 1990. The city had become home to growing Latino, Kurdish, Somali, Laotian, Vietnamese and other immigrant communities. Nashville is also often cited as having one of the largest Kurdish populations in the United States.

Opponents of the amendment said those demographic changes had helped revitalize neighborhoods, schools, churches and small businesses. Supporters said the growth made it more important for local government to set a clear expectation that English is the common language of public life.

In the end, voters sided with the opposition coalition, rejecting the proposed charter change and leaving Nashville without an English-only government rule.
